title: A new inhibitor of a bacterial phosphatase
passage: Some Gram-negative pathogens rely on periplasmic phosphatases to scavenge phosphate from their hosts, which makes these enzymes candidate drug targets. In a screen of a small-molecule library, researchers found that compound X slowed a purified periplasmic phosphatase, here called enzyme P. To learn how X acts, they characterized it from initial-rate data.

Enzyme P (2 nM) was assayed at 25 °C and pH 8.0 with the colorless substrate p-nitrophenyl phosphate (pNPP). Hydrolysis releases p-nitrophenolate, which absorbs light at 405 nm, so product formation was followed continuously in a spectrophotometer. Each initial velocity (v₀) was taken from the linear first 30 s of a reaction, during which less than 5% of the substrate was consumed. In Experiment 1, v₀ was measured at five pNPP concentrations from 0.25 to 4.0 mM, with 0, 5 or 10 µM compound X present. Compound X slowed hydrolysis at every substrate concentration tested. The results are shown as a double-reciprocal plot in Figure 1.

Experiment 2 asked whether inhibition persists after X is removed. Enzyme P (200 nM) was preincubated for 30 min with buffer or with 50 µM X. Each sample was then diluted 100-fold, either into plain assay buffer or into assay buffer that also contained 50 µM X, and its activity was measured at 2.0 mM pNPP. Every assay therefore contained 2 nM enzyme. A final reaction contained 50 µM X and 2.0 mM pNPP but no enzyme. The results are summarized in Table 1.
The researchers are now preparing to crystallize enzyme P with the compound bound.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Double-reciprocal (Lineweaver–Burk) plot of initial rates of pNPP hydrolysis by enzyme P at three concentrations of compound X. Points at 1/[S] = 0.25–4.0 mM⁻¹ are means of three replicates (SD under 5% of each mean); the points on each axis mark where the fitted line meets it.
Table 1 Activity of enzyme P at 2.0 mM pNPP after preincubation (Experiment 2), as a percentage of the buffer control; mean ± SD, n = 3.

source: Data are illustrative, constructed for practice.

questions.stem: Based on Figure 1, what are the apparent Km and Vmax of enzyme P in the presence of 10 µM compound X?
choices: Km = 0.50 mM; Vmax = 27 µM/min
Km = 0.67 mM; Vmax = 40 µM/min
Km = 1.5 mM; Vmax = 27 µM/min
Km = 1.5 mM; Vmax = 40 µM/min
why: Wrong: this is the pattern for noncompetitive inhibition (Km unchanged, Vmax lowered). In Figure 1 the 10 µM line meets the y-axis at the same 1/v₀ as the control, so Vmax is unchanged, and its slope is three times the control's, so Km is not 0.50 mM.
Wrong: 0.67 is the magnitude of the x-intercept, which is 1/Km rather than Km. Taking its reciprocal gives an apparent Km of 1.5 mM.
Wrong: Km is right, but 27 µM/min comes from reading the slope (0.0375) as 1/Vmax. The slope is Km/Vmax; Vmax comes from the y-intercept, 0.025 min/µM, which gives 40 µM/min.

Right: the y-intercept is 1/Vmax = 0.025 min/µM, so Vmax = 40 µM/min, the same as without X. The x-intercept is −1/Km = −0.667 mM⁻¹, so the apparent Km is 1.5 mM (equivalently, slope/intercept = 0.0375/0.025 = 1.5 mM).

questions.stem: The results of Experiment 1 are most consistent with compound X binding to:
choices: a site away from the active site, binding free enzyme and the ES complex equally
an active-site residue covalently, removing active enzyme molecules for good
the free enzyme's active site, so that X and substrate cannot bind at once
the enzyme–substrate complex only, so apparent Km and Vmax fall together
why: Wrong: an inhibitor that binds free enzyme and ES equally (noncompetitive) lowers Vmax with Km unchanged, so the lines would share an x-intercept. Here the x-intercepts move toward zero as [X] rises while the y-intercept stays fixed.

Wrong: removing active enzyme permanently would lower Vmax, but Vmax is unchanged in Figure 1, and Table 1 shows that activity returns to 97% of control when X is diluted away, so binding is reversible.

Right: the lines share a y-intercept (Vmax unchanged) and the apparent Km rises with [X]. That is competitive inhibition: X and substrate compete for the free enzyme's active site, so enough substrate outcompetes X.
Wrong: an inhibitor that binds only the ES complex lowers both Km and Vmax and gives parallel double-reciprocal lines. In Figure 1 the slopes differ and the lines share a y-intercept.

questions.stem: The reaction in Table 1 that contained compound X and pNPP but no enzyme was included mainly to rule out which possibility?
choices: That X lowers Vmax rather than raising the apparent Km of enzyme P
That X, or pNPP breaking down without enzyme, raises the 405 nm signal
That X stops inhibiting enzyme P once it has been diluted out of the sample
That 2.0 mM pNPP is too low a concentration to saturate enzyme P
why: Wrong: whether X changes Vmax or Km is answered by Experiment 1, which varies substrate concentration. A reaction lacking enzyme has no Vmax or Km to measure.

Right: without enzyme, any change at 405 nm would have to come from X itself or from pNPP hydrolyzing on its own in the presence of X. The rate below 1% of control shows the signal in the other assays comes from enzyme P.
Wrong: reversibility is tested by the third row of Table 1, where enzyme preincubated with X regains 97% of control activity after dilution. A reaction with no enzyme cannot address it.
Wrong: saturation is a property of the enzyme and is read from how v₀ changes with [S] in Experiment 1. A reaction with no enzyme says nothing about it.

questions.stem: Suppose the sample in the second row of Table 1, with 50 µM X in the assay, were measured at 20 mM pNPP instead of 2.0 mM and compared with a buffer control also measured at 20 mM. Its activity would most likely be:
choices: equal to 100% of the control activity
between 33% and 100% of the control activity
unchanged, still about 33% of the control activity
lower than 33% of the control activity
why: Wrong: substrate overcomes a competitive inhibitor fully only as [S] becomes far larger than the apparent Km. With an apparent Km near 5.5 mM at 50 µM X, 20 mM pNPP is not high enough.

Right: X is competitive, so raising [S] recovers activity. Figure 1 shows the apparent Km rising 0.5 mM per 5 µM X, so at 50 µM it is about 5.5 mM. At 20 mM pNPP the sample runs at about 20/25.5 = 78% of Vmax versus 98% for the control, about 80% of control.
Wrong: a fixed fraction of activity regardless of [S] is the pattern of noncompetitive inhibition, which lowers Vmax. X leaves Vmax unchanged, so its effect depends on [S].
Wrong: this reverses the effect of substrate. For a competitive inhibitor, more substrate displaces X from the active site, so the fraction of activity that remains rises.

questions.stem: Compared with the uninhibited reaction, how does adding 10 µM compound X change the hydrolysis of pNPP by enzyme P?
choices: It leaves ΔG°′ unchanged but lowers the product yield at equilibrium
It lowers Keq, so less product is present at equilibrium
It leaves Keq unchanged but slows the approach to equilibrium
It makes ΔG°′ more positive, so the reaction is less favorable
why: Wrong: this is internally inconsistent. ΔG°′ fixes Keq, so if ΔG°′ is unchanged the equilibrium yield of product is unchanged too.
Wrong: Keq is set by the free energies of substrate and products. An inhibitor, like the enzyme itself, changes only how fast equilibrium is reached.
Right: X reduces the rate of catalysis, but neither enzyme nor inhibitor changes ΔG°′ or Keq. The same equilibrium is reached, only more slowly.
Wrong: ΔG°′ is a property of the reaction, not of the catalyst. Inhibiting the enzyme slows the reaction without making it thermodynamically less favorable.
